editorial.headline: The Craft Behind a Building’s Final Character
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the floors, walls and ceilings that make buildings usable—and is fully foreign-open nationally, with no Bali moratorium block at the relevant large scale.
editorial.body:
This is the building-finishing activity that gives residential, non-residential and civil structures their completed surfaces. It concerns the work that turns a constructed shell into a usable interior or exterior: the treated wall, the finished floor underfoot, and the ceiling overhead. Its scope is practical but far from minor, because these elements determine how a completed building is experienced, protected and divided.

The work includes interior and exterior plaster and stucco finishes, along with related lining-framework materials. It also covers interior finishing such as gypsum ceilings, wooden wall coverings and removable partitions. Underfoot and across walls, the scope extends to ceramic, concrete and natural-stone coverings; parquet and other timber floors; linoleum, carpet, rubber and plastic flooring; and finishes in terrazzo, marble, granite or slate. Wallpaper and other wall coverings sit within the same activity, too. Taken together, it is a broad finishing brief rather than a narrow trade confined to one material or one room.

Businesses operating at micro, small, medium or large scale may register this activity. That range reflects the underlying nature of the work: it can be undertaken as a focused finishing assignment or as part of a substantial building-completion package. The defining question is not whether the building is residential or non-residential, nor whether the chosen surface is plaster, stone, wood, carpet or wallpaper. It is whether the business is carrying out the finishing of floors, walls or ceilings described in the activity’s scope.

Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali does not reverse that position through its permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium, which blocks low- and medium-low-risk activities. At the large scale, this activity’s OSS risk is classified as medium-high or high, and the record expressly states that it is not blocked by that moratorium. The Bali position is therefore straightforward: the activity is not marked as blocked, while the national foreign-investment position remains fully open.
editorial.pullQuote: At the large scale, the Bali moratorium does not block this activity.
